    THE HOUSE RULES

    No-limit Texas Hold’em

    Win the pot by making everyone else fold, or by holding the best five-card poker hand at showdown. Use any combination of your two private cards and the five community cards, including playing the board.

    The cash game

    You and 1–8 computer opponents occupy a fixed nine-seat table. Blinds are 5/10, the buy-in is 1,000, and there is no rake, ante, straddle, or real-money play. Positions rotate clockwise each hand. Empty seats are skipped. Computer players who bust rebuy before the next hand; you can rebuy when your stack reaches zero. Chips have no cash value.

    A hand, street by street

    1. Blinds & deal. The player left of the dealer posts the small blind and the next player posts the big blind. Each receives two private cards. Preflop action starts left of the big blind, which retains an option to raise if everyone calls.
    2. Flop. One card is burned and three community cards are dealt. Betting starts with the first remaining player left of the dealer.
    3. Turn & river. A card is burned before each of the last two community cards. Each street has another betting round.
    4. Showdown. Players still in the hand compare their best five cards. The strongest hand wins each eligible pot. If everyone but one player folds, that player wins immediately without revealing cards.

    Heads-up: the dealer posts the small blind and acts first preflop; the big blind acts first after the flop.

    Your betting options

    Fold gives up your hand and all chips committed to the pot. Check passes when you owe no chips. Call matches the current bet, or puts your remaining stack all-in if you cannot cover it. Bet / raise increases the current price. “Raise to” is your total contribution on this street, not the additional amount.

    The minimum opening bet is 10. A full raise must increase the current bet by at least the last full bet or raise increment. For example, after a raise from 10 to 30, the next minimum is 50. The maximum is your entire stack; there is no limit on the number of raises.

    A smaller raise is allowed only as an all-in. It does not reopen betting for a player who has already acted, unless the cumulative increase they face reaches the full raise required when they acted. Players who have not yet acted may still raise. After a short opening all-in, a raise must add at least 10 to that wager; there is no completion to 10. The preflop bring-in remains 10 even if the big blind has fewer chips. You cannot bet into a side pot when no opponent has chips left to contest it.

    All-ins, side pots & ties

    An all-in player can win only the chips matched by their contribution from each opponent. Extra wagers form side pots, with eligibility tracked separately. Folded chips stay in the pot. Any unmatched portion of a wager is returned. When no more betting is possible, the board runs out automatically. Eligible hands are revealed at showdown; folded cards stay hidden.

    Equal five-card hands split the pot. Suits never break ties. Remaining odd chips go to tied winners clockwise from the seat left of the dealer, separately for each pot.

    Hand rankings, strongest first

    1. Straight flush — five consecutive cards of one suit; ace-high is a royal flush.
    2. Four of a kind — four cards of one rank, then a kicker.
    3. Full house — three of a kind plus a pair; compare the trips first.
    4. Flush — five cards of one suit, compared highest to lowest.
    5. Straight — five consecutive ranks; A-2-3-4-5 is five-high.
    6. Three of a kind — three of one rank, then two kickers.
    7. Two pair — compare the higher pair, then the lower pair, then the kicker.
    8. One pair — one pair, then three kickers.
    9. High card — compare all five cards highest to lowest.

    Only five cards count. A sixth or seventh card never breaks a tie. An ace is high, except in the five-high straight.

    Saving & controls

    Every completed action saves automatically in this browser, including mid-hand. Reload to resume. Clearing browser data or starting a new table removes that session. Private browsing may not retain it. Pause stops computer actions, and Pace changes their delay. When no input or dialog is focused: F folds, C checks/calls, and R raises using the displayed total.

    The computer players estimate equity using only their own cards and the public board. They never inspect your hand or the actual deck. This is a casual, local game; the save contains the full deal so it can resume exactly.
